title: The universe in his mouth
hookLine: a mother checks her toddler's mouth for dirt and sees the whole universe inside
carry: vatsalya: the God of everything, loved as a child

cards: A toddler, a gang of bigger boys, and an accusation: he ate dirt! In the village of Gokul, the boys run to Yashoda with it. She grabs Krishna's hand and scolds him.
He looks up, all innocence: I didn't. They're lying. If you don't believe me, look for yourself.
And he opens his mouth. What Yashoda sees in there, the Bhagavata takes a whole passage to describe.

teach.b: Inside her son's mouth, the Bhagavata Purana says, Yashoda sees everything. The sky and all its directions. Stars and planets.
Mountains, islands, oceans. Wind and fire and the moon.
And somewhere in all that, the village of Gokul, and in it, herself, standing there looking into her son's mouth. She's shaken to the core. Is this a dream?
A trick? Or is this child something beyond anything I can understand? She begins, the text says, to take refuge in the one whose nature is beyond thought.
Then the story does something tender. Krishna, the text says, spreads his power of affection over her, the covering the tradition calls maya, and she forgets. The vision fades.
She takes him back on her lap. She's just his mother again, he's just her little boy, and she loves him more than ever. Here's what that means for the bhakti road.
The vision was real. But Krishna didn't want Yashoda trembling before the cosmic Lord. He wanted to be held and scolded and fed.

teach.h: HE'D RATHER BE HELD THAN FEARED.
teach.b: Devotees in Krishna traditions often say this is the heart of it: God enjoys being loved as a child, a friend, a beloved, more than being feared as a king.

teach.h: THE UNIVERSE FITS IN HIS MOUTH.
teach.b: The universe fits in his mouth. And he'd rather sit in your lap. This mood has a name, vatsalya, loving God the way a parent loves a child, and it's why at Janmashtami families rock baby Krishna in a little cradle.

how: Devotees of Krishna retell the stories of his childhood in Gokul and Vrindavan in songs, dance and festival plays, especially at Janmashtami, and many relate to him with vatsalya, the tender love of a parent for a child.

o: a cosmic vision that only gods can see
action, like a mother crouching down to look
the reward a devotee earns for worship

games.q: inside his mouth — tap the pairs.
p: looked in and saw the universe

s: Yashoda sees herself inside Krishna's mouth
among the stars and oceans, she sees Gokul, and herself looking in.
after the vision, Yashoda worships Krishna only as a king
the vision fades, and she's his mother again, loving him more than ever.
the story comes from the Bhagavata Purana
from its tenth part, the stories of Krishna's childhood.

games.q: you're Yashoda. you've just seen the entire universe inside your toddler's mouth. what happens next in the story?
o: you bow down and never treat him as your child again.
you run and tell the whole village.
the vision fades, you forget, and you hold him in your lap.
games.why: Krishna covers her with affection and she forgets. devotees say he'd rather be loved as a child than feared as a king.

practice: Think of something enormous, the night sky, the ocean, the number of people alive right now, and let it be too big to hold.
Then bring something small close, the way Yashoda held her child: your own hands, a cup of tea, a face you love, and let the enormous and the near sit together.
If you pray, you can speak to God as someone close, not only someone vast.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and today the action is a mother's: crouching down, looking in, and loving him anyway.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tender love, as of a parent for a child (from vatsa, a calf). One of the moods of bhakti.

carryVoice: Carry this: vatsalya, the God of everything, loved as a child. Whole worlds inside, and still a little boy. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.8.32–10.8.45 (the universe in Krishna's mouth)
